title: How an application looks up a name

blocks.body: Applications do not speak DNS. They call `getaddrinfo()`, which checks `/etc/hosts` first and only then asks DNS through the stub resolver. Tools like `dig` skip the first step, so they can disagree with what an application sees.
The chain `application -> getaddrinfo() -> /etc/hosts -> stub resolver -> nameserver`. The first source that returns an address wins.
`/etc/hosts` predates DNS and still allows local overrides (e.g. `localhost`). DNS is consulted for everything else.

glibc follows the `hosts:` line of `/etc/nsswitch.conf` (usually `files dns`). musl (Alpine, this lab) has no NSS: it always reads `/etc/hosts`, then `/etc/resolv.conf`, then sends the DNS query. `strace` makes this visible as `openat("/etc/hosts")`, `openat("/etc/resolv.conf")` and a `sendto(...port 53...)`.
`getent hosts api.shop.example` uses the same path as `curl`. `dig api.shop.example` asks DNS only. If `getent` succeeds but `dig` fails, the answer is coming from `/etc/hosts`.

- `getent hosts <name>`: the application's view.
- `dig <name>`: the DNS view.
- `cat /etc/hosts`: local overrides.
- `strace -f -e trace=openat,sendto,connect getent hosts <name>`: the files read and the packets sent.

- A stale `/etc/hosts` entry hides a DNS change.
- Pinning an address in `/etc/hosts` "fixes" one name on one host and hides a broken resolver.
- Testing with `dig` and concluding the application must work (or must fail).
